title: Kernel jam quant chaos scan — signal decomposition & mitigation notes
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a focused investigation into repeated, transient latency spikes we saw on INT8 and AWQ kernels during multiworkload bursts. The working hypothesis is a short-lived kernel-level resource contention I call a 'kernel jam' — not full queue saturation but micro-contention across vector lanes, memory banks, and scheduler slots leading to 10–40ms tail spikes on p50->p95 hops. This doc records the signal decomposition approach, probes run, raw observations, and short mitigation ideas to test in the runtime.

Background / why this matters:
- Customers see occasional user-facing stalls even when aggregate throughput looks fine.
- Existing batching and KV caching reduce avg cost but don't eliminate short spikes that break tight latency SLOs (e.g., 99th percentile chat latency).
- Spikes are more prominent on low-precision kernels (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ) and on mixed-quant deployments where some layers use different kernels.

What I mean by 'kernel jam':
- Concurrent requests trigger different kernel variants (e.g., AWQ-optimized kernel vs generic int8 kernel) mapped onto the same execution units.
- Micro-scheduling causes interleaved vector lane usage + memory bank prefetch patterns to misalign; small windows of reduced arithmetic throughput or cache thrash appear as spikes.
- Not a deterministic bug; signal appears stochastically depending on sequence length distribution and micro-batching timing.

Signal decomposition methodology (how we instrumented):
1) End-to-end trace correlation
   - Collect request-level traces with timestamps for: enqueue, kernel-launch, kernel-complete, post-processing.
   - Annotate with model variant, quant profile (int8/gptq/awq/fp8), and batchshape.
2) Tracing the GPU timeline
   - nvprof / Nsight timeline captures per-kernel start/end, SM utilization, mem throughput.
   - Instrument runtime to emit micro-events (KV cache hit/miss, tile assembly, kernel-select decision).
3) Microbench harness
   - Local harness that replays representative request traces at scale but with controlled inter-arrival jitter.
   - Ability to force kernel mix (e.g., 60% AWQ, 40% GPTQ) to recreate contention.
4) Frequency-domain analysis
   - Convert sequence of kernel latencies into time series and run short-window FFT to detect periodic jam signatures (we saw energy at 5–12Hz in some workloads).

Probes & experiments run:
- Baseline: single-model single-kernel steady replay (INT8) — p95 stable, no spikes.
- Mixed-kernel probe: interleave AWQ and generic INT8 requests with slight offset jitter (0–5ms). Result: reproducible ~15–35ms spikes at p99 when two kernels start within a 1–3ms window.
- Bank-stress probe: run synthetic matmul-heavy microkernels targeting same memory banks. Result: sharp drop in achieved FLOPS during jam windows; Nsight shows lower SM occupancy but sustained L2 utilization and rising global mem latency.
- Warm-up shift probe: add a warmup request stream with long prefix (cache-heavy) while normal traffic runs; observed increased tail spikes — suggests combined effect of cache reallocation + kernel switchover.

Representative numbers (example workload: 1.3B model, seq 1024, batch 1–4):
- Steady single-kernel INT8 run: p50 18ms, p95 28ms, p99 45ms.
- Mixed AWQ/INT8 replay (50/50): p50 20ms, p95 36ms, p99 85ms, intermittent spikes to 120ms.
- With targeted mitigation (see below): p50 19ms, p95 30ms, p99 52ms.

Low-level observations from traces:
- Kernel start times that collide within <2ms windows correlate with spikes.
- During jam windows, kernel durations inflate by 1.5–3x for specific kernels, while others are unaffected.
- Nsight: SM utilization dips but memory pipes show backlog (higher DRAM latency).
- L2 cache eviction patterns: warmup requests cause large tiles to touch L2, evicting small working sets used by short requests, forcing extra DRAM roundtrips for those lanes.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Memory-bank / L2 eviction interaction between long-prefix warmups and short requests leads to extra memory latency for some kernels.
2) Scheduling quant-kernel variants onto the same CU warps causes suboptimal instruction mix (some kernels are fused ops benefiting from vector-wide instructions; when interleaved, they lose vectorization density).
3) Driver-level kernel queueing reorders launches in a way that increases head-of-line blocking under micro-burst patterns.

Initial mitigation ideas (fast experiments):
- Kernel pinning per-request-class: route short interactive requests to a small pool running a single kernel variant (no mixing). Pros: eliminates mix-contention; Cons: reduces overall utilization.
- Micro-burst smoothing: introduce 1–2ms jitter/deferral for low-priority requests to avoid tight-start collisions. Easy to test in scheduler.
- L2-friendly tiling: change tiling in the warmup path to avoid bulk L2 evictions (smaller tiles, prefetch hints). Expected to reduce DRAM miss storms.
- Kernel batching alignment: ensure that co-launched kernels align vector lanes so fused ops keep density. This is more invasive (kernel generation/runtime cooperation).

Tests run and short results:
- Pinning test: create two dedicated GPU streams (poolA short requests, poolB warmups). Result: p99 reduced from 85ms -> 52ms; p95 similar to baseline. Utilization dropped ~8%.
- Jitter test: add 0–3ms random jitter on short request dispatch. Result: reduced collision frequency by ~70% and p99 by ~30% with negligible utilization impact.
- L2 tiling test (simulated in microkernel): smaller tile reduced eviction footprint; reduced p99 in mixed workload by ~22%.

Actionable next steps to validate in prod-like cluster:
1) Run a 48h canary with jitter enabled on selected routes (low risk). Monitor p50/p95/p99 and utilization metrics.
2) Implement and A/B kernel pinning on dedicated pool for one critical route with conservative capacity guardrails.
3) Add a kernel-launch collision metric to tracing (time-delta to previous kernel on same CU) and alert when collision frequency exceeds threshold.
4) Work with kernel engineers to explore a tiled prefetch mode for warmup kernels.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How does FP8 behave in identical mixes? We saw fewer spikes in one small probe, but need systematic runs because FP8 kernels sometimes have different memory patterns.
- Are there driver-side knobs (CUDA streams/priority, MPS behavior) that deterministically reorder launches — can we influence order without major infra changes?
- Longer-term: can the compiler emit kernel variants resilient to interleaving (e.g., preserve vector density when partially issued)?

Notes to reviewers:
- Attachments: raw replay traces (S3 links), Nsight slices, and the probe harness with configuration used.
- This is a working doc — lots of rough numbers. Please comment if you have a perf tool that can export per-interval L2 eviction heatmaps; that would help.

Appendix: quick commands used (local harness)
- capture trace: ./harness --replay trace.json --emit-events /tmp/trace.events
- nsight capture: nsight-sys --capture=short --output=nsight.sess -- ./runtime --load-config small
- microkernel perf: ./microbench --kernel awq --tile 64 --iters 5000 --report-counters

Short ack: Marcus ran the jitter canary on a test node and saw immediate improvement. Sofia is driving the tiled warmup prototype. Ethan will open the tracing PR to add collision metrics.
